The Challenge of Uncontrolled Water Costs

The familiar version goes like this. A property receives a bulk water invoice that's well above budget. The building team checks for obvious failures, asks maintenance to listen for running toilets, and sends a general reminder to residents about conservation. The next bill arrives and the number still doesn't make sense.

That's the weakness of a master-metered building. You know the property consumed water, but you don't know where, by whom, or whether the spike came from resident behaviour, a concealed leak, irrigation drift, a make-up water issue, or common-area waste. Finance sees expense growth. Operations sees guesswork.

For boards and ownership groups, the pain isn't just the invoice itself. It's the lack of control. A utility cost that can't be traced is hard to recover, hard to forecast, and hard to challenge. It also creates tenant friction because everyone subsidises the heaviest users when water is embedded in rent or common expenses.
Unmeasured consumption almost always turns into delayed action. By the time a building team sees the master bill, the waste has already happened.

Outdoor use can make the problem worse. If your property has maintained grounds, irrigation may be part of the story, and it should be reviewed alongside indoor consumption. A practical companion resource is this
guide to maximizing irrigation ROI
, which looks at how owners can tie water conservation decisions to operating performance rather than treating grounds maintenance as a separate silo.

Sub metered water solves a basic management problem. It gives the property a measurable line of sight between consumption, cost allocation, and maintenance response. Once that visibility exists, the water bill stops being a monthly surprise and starts becoming something the team can manage.
What Is Sub Metered Water

A board usually sees one water line on the operating statement. The building, however, uses water in dozens or hundreds of places. Sub metered water closes that gap by measuring consumption at the unit, tenant, or use-area level instead of relying only on the master meter.

The property still receives utility service through a main meter. Submeters sit downstream and record actual usage for apartments, tenant suites, irrigation zones, cooling makeup lines, laundry rooms, or other defined loads. That shift matters because it turns water from a pooled expense into a managed asset category with traceable consumption, clearer recovery, and faster maintenance response.
From one master bill to unit level visibility

With a master-meter-only setup, ownership gets a total. Useful accounting starts there, but operational control does not. True submetering adds a second layer of information that lets teams assign costs accurately, isolate common-area use, investigate sudden spikes, and spot losses before they roll through another billing cycle.

children.text: In practice, owners use that visibility in four ways:
Usage-based billing.
Charges can be tied to measured consumption instead of broad allocations.
Leak and exception detection.
Overnight flow, continuous low-volume use, or sudden jumps in one line can point to a running toilet, failed valve, or concealed leak.
Common-area separation.
Teams can distinguish resident consumption from irrigation, amenities, and house loads.
Asset analytics.
Managers can review unit, stack, and building trends to target maintenance dollars where they will protect NOI.
That is why many owners now evaluate
water submetering solutions for multifamily and commercial properties

as part of a wider operating strategy, not as a billing add-on. The better systems support installation, data collection, alerts, billing workflows, and ongoing service in one program. That reduces handoffs and gives finance and operations a shared record of where water is going.
Why true submetering is not the same as RUBS
Boards should separate submetering from RUBS early because they solve different problems.
RUBS
, or Ratio Utility Billing System, allocates a master bill using a formula such as occupancy, unit count, or square footage.
Submetering
measures actual use in each unit or defined area.

That difference affects more than resident billing. Actual measurement gives teams data they can act on. Formula allocation does not show which unit has continuous flow, which stack is drifting upward, or whether a common-area load is driving the increase. If the goal is stronger cost recovery, fairer resident charges, and better control of leaks and waste, measurement gives the property a much stronger operating tool.

California adds another layer of complexity. There, owners need to distinguish true submetering from RUBS carefully because sewer charges are often tied to the master meter. True sewer submetering can be difficult without specific local agreements. Misclassifying RUBS as submetering can create CPUC exposure and tenant disputes, as outlined in the
San Francisco Public Utilities Commission residential submetering FAQs
Practical rule:
If the system does not measure actual unit use, treat it as an allocation method, not a metering strategy.

That distinction matters at approval time. A billing formula may recover some cost. A metering system gives the asset a usable data layer for leak response, budgeting, capital planning, and compliance. For owners focused on preserving NOI and reducing avoidable property risk, that is the definition of sub metered water.
The Core Benefits for Property Owners

A master bill lands 22% above budget, maintenance cannot explain the spike, and by the time the team finds the cause, one leaking toilet and a failed irrigation valve have already turned into avoidable expense. That is the operating problem sub metered water solves. Cost recovery matters, but the larger value is control. Owners get a usable data layer for protecting NOI, tightening site operations, and reducing water-related property risk.

children.text: NOI protection starts with accountability

Unit-level measurement changes the financial model of the asset. When water is bundled into rent, the owner carries both the consumption risk and the resident behavior risk. With submetering, a larger share of utility cost becomes recoverable, variance is easier to explain, and budget discussions get more grounded in actual use instead of assumptions.

The conservation effect also has practical value for boards. As noted earlier in the article, industry research has found materially lower consumption in submetered properties than in communities where water is included in rent. For an owner, that shows up as lower bulk demand, fewer spikes that need explanation, and better confidence in annual utility forecasting.

Resident fairness matters here too. Actual-use billing is easier to defend than broad allocation formulas in buildings with different household sizes, work-from-home patterns, or uneven occupancy. Fewer billing disputes means less staff time spent on exceptions and collections.
A typical benefit stack looks like this:
Priority
Owner outcome
Why it matters
Cost recovery
Better alignment between use and charges
Reduces pressure on operating margins
Budget control
Fewer surprises on the master bill
Improves forecasting and board reporting
Resident fairness
Users pay based on consumption
Cuts disputes over shared costs
Data visibility
Faster identification of anomalies
Supports maintenance and capital planning
The strongest operators do not stop at billing. They add
integrated leak detection for multifamily water systems
because the largest loss is often not the water itself. It is the drywall, flooring, downtime, resident disruption, and claim activity that follow a leak no one caught early.
The operational upside most owners miss

Submetering should be evaluated as an asset management system. The meter data helps teams spot abnormal flow, isolate recurring trouble units, compare buildings across a portfolio, and decide whether a problem belongs in routine maintenance or the capital plan.

That changes response time. A property team can move from “the bill looks high this month” to “Unit 304 has continuous overnight flow and Building B's domestic line is trending above baseline.” That is a very different operating position.
The financial effect is straightforward:
Less avoidable water loss
lowers operating expense pressure.
Earlier leak detection
reduces the size of repairs and the chance of multi-unit damage.
Clearer usage records
help document timelines, resident responsibility, and vendor response.
Portfolio trend data
supports better planning for plumbing replacements, fixture upgrades, and reserve decisions.

Older properties see this value fastest because hidden waste and deferred plumbing issues are more common there. In those assets, submetering often pays back in two ways. First through improved recovery and lower consumption. Second through incident prevention, which protects NOI less conspicuously but often more materially.

Boards usually approve submetering for utility savings. The better reason is risk control. Owners who use it as part of the property's operating discipline get stronger forecasting, faster leak response, better documentation, and fewer avoidable hits to margin.
Navigating Technical and Regulatory Requirements

The technical side intimidates some boards because they picture a specialised system with a lot of code risk and tenant sensitivity. In reality, the process is manageable when the equipment, installer, and billing model are aligned to the jurisdiction.
What the equipment choice means in practice

At the property level, the key technical decision isn't just meter type. It's whether the whole system supports accurate measurement, reliable reads, serviceability, and clean data transfer into billing and reporting. Owners don't need to become meter engineers, but they do need enough understanding to ask useful questions.
A workable shortlist usually includes:
Meter suitability:
The meter has to fit the pipe conditions, unit layout, and access constraints of the building.
Read method:
Remote data collection is much more practical than manual read programmes in occupied properties.
Service access:
Meters should be replaceable and testable without turning routine maintenance into a major resident coordination exercise.
Alerting capability:
Leak and abnormal-use notifications are where operational value starts compounding.
The wrong equipment choice doesn't usually fail on day one. It fails later, when reads become inconsistent, access becomes painful, or billing exceptions start piling up.
That's why technical design should be tied to how the property runs. A high-rise rental, a stacked townhouse site, and a mixed-use asset won't have the same installation logic or support needs.
Ontario and California show how compliance really works

Ontario and California are useful examples because they show two different regulatory styles. Ontario's framework is tied to building and tenancy rules. California adds a strong measurement and certification layer for billing-grade submeters.

In Ontario, water submetering is governed by the Building Code and the Residential Tenancies Act. It doesn't require the same OEB licensing structure that applies to electricity submetering, but it still has to comply with installation and billing rules that support fairness and transparency, as described in this overview of
Ontario water submetering under the OBC and RTA
. For boards, that means implementation is not informal. Rent treatment, billing practices, and installation standards all need to be handled correctly.

California is more prescriptive on meter compliance. Water submeters used for tenant billing must be type-approved, tested, sealed, and registered with the local County Weights and Measures agency before installation. They must also be installed by properly qualified parties, and recertification requirements can affect long-term operations, according to the
California Apartment Association summary of water submeter requirements
A practical board-level takeaway is simple. Compliance is not a side task after installation. It's part of project design.
Jurisdiction
Main concern for owners
Operational implication
Ontario
Building and tenancy compliance
Billing setup and tenant treatment must be planned properly
California
Meter approval, installation, and certification
Provider selection must account for testing, sealing, and recertification requirements

When a provider manages permits, certifications, billing logic, and resident-facing processes together, the project gets easier to govern. When those responsibilities are fragmented, the owner usually ends up coordinating risk that should have been managed upstream.
Implementation Timeline and Cost Models
A submetering project becomes easier to approve when the board can see the sequence clearly. Most hesitation comes from uncertainty around disruption, resident access, and who pays for what.
What a real project rollout looks like

A typical rollout starts with a site review and scope confirmation. The provider or project team looks at plumbing configuration, unit count, access conditions, common-area separation, communications method, and billing requirements. From there, the system is designed around the building rather than forced into a standard template.

children.text: The working stages usually look like this:
Assessment and design
The property is reviewed for technical fit, code requirements, meter locations, and billing structure.
Installation planning
Access notices, trade coordination, equipment scheduling, and resident communications are lined up.
Physical installation
Meters and sensors are installed, tested, and connected to the data platform.
Commissioning
Reads are verified, exceptions are checked, and the billing environment is prepared.
Go-live and support
Billing starts, residents receive account information, and ongoing monitoring begins.
Axis Meter Solutions, for example, describes a typical
8 to 10 week
timeline from agreement to live meters and uses a
$0 upfront

provider-owned model with ongoing maintenance under a long-term agreement. Those project details come from the company information provided for this article, not from an external study, and they're useful because they show what a turnkey structure can look like in practice.
How owners usually structure the cost
Boards generally compare two models.
The first is the
capital expenditure model

. The owner buys the equipment, pays for installation, and then either runs billing internally or hires separate service partners. This gives the owner direct asset ownership, but it also keeps maintenance, replacements, data support, and resident billing complexity closer to the property team.
The second is the
provider-owned service model

. In that structure, the provider supplies equipment, manages installation and commissioning, handles billing workflows, and maintains the system over the term. That can remove the upfront capital barrier and reduce administrative load.
The trade-off isn't mysterious:
Capex model:
More direct ownership, more internal responsibility.
Service model:
Less upfront spend, more dependence on contract quality and provider performance.
Boards should approve the operating model, not just the hardware. The wrong contract can erase the advantage of the right meter.

Good due diligence focuses on practical questions. Who handles resident support? Who pays for replacement meters? Who manages leaks, billing disputes, and compliance updates? How quickly can a failed device be restored to service? Those answers affect the actual cost far more than the meter price alone.
ROI in Action Real World Examples
The most persuasive ROI discussions don't rely on flashy case studies. They look at where the financial return is evident in an operating statement and in maintenance records.
Where the return usually appears first

In most portfolios, the first gains come from three places. The owner stops absorbing all usage indiscriminately. Building staff get clearer signals about abnormal consumption. And leaks that would otherwise sit unnoticed become visible earlier.
That third point matters more in older stock. In California, where aging infrastructure is common, unmonitored leaks can account for
over 15% of total water consumption
, and submetering paired with leak detection has reduced water loss incidents by
40% in multi-family units
, according to the source referenced earlier in the article. If you want to review how providers present actual project outcomes, use
submetering case studies
as a comparison tool, but evaluate them for operating logic, not marketing language.
Examples boards immediately understand

Consider a mid-rise rental building with a recurring problem on the master bill. Before submetering, management can only react after total consumption has already hit the utility invoice. After unit-level measurement is installed, the team can identify outlier suites, separate common-area use, and see whether the issue is behavioural or mechanical. The immediate return is better cost allocation. The secondary return is faster maintenance response.

A condominium corporation often faces a different issue. The board may be less focused on direct rent recovery and more focused on fairness, owner accountability, and long-term infrastructure discipline. In that setting, sub metered water improves governance because the board no longer has to defend broad cost-sharing when actual use varies sharply from one suite to another.

A mixed-use property usually sees the value in separation. Residential, retail, and common-area demands don't behave the same way. When all of that sits behind one water bill, the owner loses clarity. When those streams are measured separately, the asset becomes easier to budget and easier to explain to both commercial tenants and residential occupants.
A board doesn't need a dramatic case study to justify the decision. It needs confidence that the programme will do four things consistently:
Recover costs more cleanly
Expose leaks sooner
Reduce billing disputes
Improve operating visibility
Those are not theoretical wins. They are the mechanics of protecting NOI in a building where water has been treated as a shared, opaque expense for too long.
Choosing Your Submetering Partner

A poor vendor choice rarely fails on installation day. It fails six months later, when a leak alert goes nowhere, a resident disputes a bill, or the board asks for a clean report on common-area consumption and no one can produce it. At that point, water submetering stops being a capital project and becomes an operating problem.

body.alt: An infographic titled Selecting Your Submetering Partner listing five key criteria for choosing a submetering provider.

children.text: The right partner helps protect NOI in three ways. The firm must keep billing accurate, turn meter data into maintenance action, and reduce the administrative load on the site team. Hardware matters, but boards usually feel the financial difference in service execution, compliance handling, and response discipline.
What to ask before you sign

Start with operating accountability, not just meter specifications. A board should know who owns each part of the program after installation, how exceptions are handled, and what recourse exists if service levels slip.
Regulatory fit
Ask how the provider handles local billing rules, meter approvals, testing requirements, disclosures, and recordkeeping. Water revenue is only defensible if the process holds up under local rules.
Hardware standards
Confirm the meters are approved for billing use where the property operates. Get clear language on device life, replacement cycles, calibration, and who pays when equipment fails.
Data and alerting

Require a clear explanation of what the ownership group, manager, and maintenance team can see. Unit consumption, common-area use, exception reporting, and leak alerts should feed a defined response process.
Billing operations

Clarify who issues invoices, answers resident questions, manages disputes, and tracks collections. If those tasks fall back to on-site staff, the proposal is shifting operating cost back to the owner.
Insurance and risk transfer
Review insurance coverage, service obligations, access protocols, and fault allocation. If a leak is detected but not acted on, the contract should make responsibilities clear.

Axis Meter Solutions is one example of a turnkey provider in this category, covering utility submetering, billing, maintenance, and leak and flood detection under long-term service agreements. The point is not the brand. The point is the model. Boards should compare full-scope providers against firms that install meters but leave reporting, resident support, or exception management with the property team.
Why service scope matters as much as hardware

Two proposals can look nearly identical in procurement. Both may include meter supply, installation, and billing. The gap shows up after go-live, when the property needs a leak escalated at 2 a.m., a disputed bill documented properly, or a year-end consumption report broken out in a way finance can use.
That is where the asset management value is won or lost.

A strong submetering partner does more than allocate charges. The provider should help the ownership group spot abnormal consumption early, separate tenant-caused costs from building-system issues, and create records that support budgeting, reserve planning, and risk control. Done well, submetering becomes part of how the asset is managed, not just how utility costs are passed through.
Use this test during diligence:
Question
What a good answer sounds like
Who owns maintenance responsibility?
Responsibility is assigned clearly, with service times and escalation steps documented
How are billing issues handled?
There is a defined resident support process, with tracking and dispute resolution procedures
What happens if regulations change?
The provider monitors rule changes and updates billing and compliance procedures accordingly
How are leaks escalated?
Alerts route to a named action protocol tied to maintenance response, follow-up, and documentation
Choose the partner you would trust during a billing dispute, an audit request, or a flood event.

That standard usually leads boards away from the lowest meter price and toward the provider with better controls, clearer reporting, and stronger follow-through. Over the life of the program, those factors have a bigger effect on operating efficiency, avoidable water loss, and management burden than a small difference in upfront equipment cost.

When a provider manages permits, certifications, billing logic, and resident-facing processes together, the project gets easier to govern. When those responsibilities are fragmented, the owner usually ends up coordinating risk that should have been managed upstream.

Implementation Timeline and Cost Models

A submetering project becomes easier to approve when the board can see the sequence clearly. Most hesitation comes from uncertainty around disruption, resident access, and who pays for what.

What a real project rollout looks like

A typical rollout starts with a site review and scope confirmation. The provider or project team looks at plumbing configuration, unit count, access conditions, common-area separation, communications method, and billing requirements. From there, the system is designed around the building rather than forced into a standard template.

The working stages usually look like this:

  1. Assessment and design
    The property is reviewed for technical fit, code requirements, meter locations, and billing structure.

  2. Installation planning
    Access notices, trade coordination, equipment scheduling, and resident communications are lined up.

  3. Physical installation
    Meters and sensors are installed, tested, and connected to the data platform.

  4. Commissioning
    Reads are verified, exceptions are checked, and the billing environment is prepared.

  5. Go-live and support
    Billing starts, residents receive account information, and ongoing monitoring begins.

Axis Meter Solutions, for example, describes a typical 8 to 10 week timeline from agreement to live meters and uses a $0 upfront provider-owned model with ongoing maintenance under a long-term agreement. Those project details come from the company information provided for this article, not from an external study, and they're useful because they show what a turnkey structure can look like in practice.

How owners usually structure the cost

Boards generally compare two models.

The first is the capital expenditure model. The owner buys the equipment, pays for installation, and then either runs billing internally or hires separate service partners. This gives the owner direct asset ownership, but it also keeps maintenance, replacements, data support, and resident billing complexity closer to the property team.

The second is the provider-owned service model. In that structure, the provider supplies equipment, manages installation and commissioning, handles billing workflows, and maintains the system over the term. That can remove the upfront capital barrier and reduce administrative load.

The trade-off isn't mysterious:

  • Capex model: More direct ownership, more internal responsibility.
  • Service model: Less upfront spend, more dependence on contract quality and provider performance.

Boards should approve the operating model, not just the hardware. The wrong contract can erase the advantage of the right meter.

Good due diligence focuses on practical questions. Who handles resident support? Who pays for replacement meters? Who manages leaks, billing disputes, and compliance updates? How quickly can a failed device be restored to service? Those answers affect the actual cost far more than the meter price alone.

ROI in Action Real World Examples

The most persuasive ROI discussions don't rely on flashy case studies. They look at where the financial return is evident in an operating statement and in maintenance records.

Where the return usually appears first

In most portfolios, the first gains come from three places. The owner stops absorbing all usage indiscriminately. Building staff get clearer signals about abnormal consumption. And leaks that would otherwise sit unnoticed become visible earlier.

That third point matters more in older stock. In California, where aging infrastructure is common, unmonitored leaks can account for over 15% of total water consumption, and submetering paired with leak detection has reduced water loss incidents by 40% in multi-family units, according to the source referenced earlier in the article. If you want to review how providers present actual project outcomes, use submetering case studies as a comparison tool, but evaluate them for operating logic, not marketing language.

Examples boards immediately understand

Consider a mid-rise rental building with a recurring problem on the master bill. Before submetering, management can only react after total consumption has already hit the utility invoice. After unit-level measurement is installed, the team can identify outlier suites, separate common-area use, and see whether the issue is behavioural or mechanical. The immediate return is better cost allocation. The secondary return is faster maintenance response.

A condominium corporation often faces a different issue. The board may be less focused on direct rent recovery and more focused on fairness, owner accountability, and long-term infrastructure discipline. In that setting, sub metered water improves governance because the board no longer has to defend broad cost-sharing when actual use varies sharply from one suite to another.

A mixed-use property usually sees the value in separation. Residential, retail, and common-area demands don't behave the same way. When all of that sits behind one water bill, the owner loses clarity. When those streams are measured separately, the asset becomes easier to budget and easier to explain to both commercial tenants and residential occupants.

A board doesn't need a dramatic case study to justify the decision. It needs confidence that the programme will do four things consistently:

  • Recover costs more cleanly
  • Expose leaks sooner
  • Reduce billing disputes
  • Improve operating visibility

Those are not theoretical wins. They are the mechanics of protecting NOI in a building where water has been treated as a shared, opaque expense for too long.

Choosing Your Submetering Partner

A poor vendor choice rarely fails on installation day. It fails six months later, when a leak alert goes nowhere, a resident disputes a bill, or the board asks for a clean report on common-area consumption and no one can produce it. At that point, water submetering stops being a capital project and becomes an operating problem.

The right partner helps protect NOI in three ways. The firm must keep billing accurate, turn meter data into maintenance action, and reduce the administrative load on the site team. Hardware matters, but boards usually feel the financial difference in service execution, compliance handling, and response discipline.

What to ask before you sign

Start with operating accountability, not just meter specifications. A board should know who owns each part of the program after installation, how exceptions are handled, and what recourse exists if service levels slip.

  • Regulatory fit
    Ask how the provider handles local billing rules, meter approvals, testing requirements, disclosures, and recordkeeping. Water revenue is only defensible if the process holds up under local rules.

  • Hardware standards
    Confirm the meters are approved for billing use where the property operates. Get clear language on device life, replacement cycles, calibration, and who pays when equipment fails.

  • Data and alerting
    Require a clear explanation of what the ownership group, manager, and maintenance team can see. Unit consumption, common-area use, exception reporting, and leak alerts should feed a defined response process.

  • Billing operations
    Clarify who issues invoices, answers resident questions, manages disputes, and tracks collections. If those tasks fall back to on-site staff, the proposal is shifting operating cost back to the owner.

  • Insurance and risk transfer
    Review insurance coverage, service obligations, access protocols, and fault allocation. If a leak is detected but not acted on, the contract should make responsibilities clear.

Axis Meter Solutions is one example of a turnkey provider in this category, covering utility submetering, billing, maintenance, and leak and flood detection under long-term service agreements. The point is not the brand. The point is the model. Boards should compare full-scope providers against firms that install meters but leave reporting, resident support, or exception management with the property team.

Why service scope matters as much as hardware

Two proposals can look nearly identical in procurement. Both may include meter supply, installation, and billing. The gap shows up after go-live, when the property needs a leak escalated at 2 a.m., a disputed bill documented properly, or a year-end consumption report broken out in a way finance can use.

That is where the asset management value is won or lost.

A strong submetering partner does more than allocate charges. The provider should help the ownership group spot abnormal consumption early, separate tenant-caused costs from building-system issues, and create records that support budgeting, reserve planning, and risk control. Done well, submetering becomes part of how the asset is managed, not just how utility costs are passed through.

Use this test during diligence:

Question What a good answer sounds like
Who owns maintenance responsibility? Responsibility is assigned clearly, with service times and escalation steps documented
How are billing issues handled? There is a defined resident support process, with tracking and dispute resolution procedures
What happens if regulations change? The provider monitors rule changes and updates billing and compliance procedures accordingly
How are leaks escalated? Alerts route to a named action protocol tied to maintenance response, follow-up, and documentation

Choose the partner you would trust during a billing dispute, an audit request, or a flood event.

That standard usually leads boards away from the lowest meter price and toward the provider with better controls, clearer reporting, and stronger follow-through. Over the life of the program, those factors have a bigger effect on operating efficiency, avoidable water loss, and management burden than a small difference in upfront equipment cost.
